The two competitive eaters engaged in an official "staredown," locking eyes in a prolonged and menacing exchange.

At last year's contest, 25-year-old Chestnut, a civil engineering student at San Jose State University, narrowly defeated Kobayashi, 31, in a tiebreaker after both men had consumed 59 hot dogs apiece. This marked Chestnut's second consecutive—if slender—victory over his Japanese rival. Kobayashi has vowed to avenge these back-to-back defeats on Saturday, adding that he no longer suffers from the so-called "jawthritis" that some blamed for his 2007 loss, which ended his remarkable six-year winning streak at Coney Island.

For his part, Chestnut expressed no intention of relinquishing the coveted mustard-yellow belt—competitive eating's equivalent of golf's green jacket—and has set his sights on consuming 68 hot dogs within the contest's 10-minute window. Saturday's showdown carries an added element of redemption for Chestnut as well: in May, he suffered a bruising defeat to Kobayashi, a loss he described as having "really set a fire underneath me" and "made me hungry for this contest."

Chestnut also disclosed the rigorous dietary regimen he has adopted in the days preceding the competition, explaining that he is consuming only water to ensure he is completely "empty" once the towering pile of hot dogs is placed before him. Meanwhile, Kobayashi acknowledged keeping a close watch not only on Chestnut but also on 32-year-old Tim "Eater X" Janus, whose distinctive painted face was characterized by Major League Eating impresario Richard Shea as a veiled attempt to conceal his "inner torment." In a recent trial run, Janus set a personal best of 55 hot dogs—just shy of the 59 consumed by both Chestnut and Kobayashi last year.

As a prelude to the main event, Major League Eating will host an unprecedented "cross-species" eating contest on Friday, pitting three competitive eaters against three Asian elephants. Shea described the event as the fulfillment of one of his two lifelong ambitions—the other being to witness a dozen competitive eaters consume the entire contents of a convenience store.

Twenty finalists, selected from a field of competitors across 18 preliminary contests, will vie for the championship title on Saturday, representing a veritable Who's Who of the competitive eating world. # Stomachs of Steel: Inside the Bizarre World of Competitive Hot Dog Training

Every Fourth of July, the world's most gifted digestive systems converge on Coney Island to answer humanity's most pressing question: how many hot dogs can a human being eat in ten minutes? The answer keeps climbing, and the training methods behind it are getting stranger by the year.

## The Elephant in the Room

Perhaps no piece of competitive eating lore is stranger than the legend of Bob Shoudt allegedly training by eating like an elephant would—stuffing himself with massive quantities of low-calorie bulk (think cabbage, watermelon, whatever's cheap and voluminous) to physically stretch stomach capacity before switching to the real target food. The logic, such as it is: teach your stomach that "full" is a moving target. Whether or not actual pachyderms were involved or merely elephant-sized portions, the technique reflects a genuine training philosophy in the sport—capacity is trainable, and gut elasticity is basically a competitive advantage you build like a bicep.

## The Physics of a Body That Shouldn't Work This Way

What's genuinely fascinating is the disconnect between competitor size and competitor performance. You'd assume the largest humans would dominate, but competitive eating rewards something closer to a hollow-legged marathoner's build. Joey Chestnut, the sport's reigning legend, competes at a fairly unremarkable 6'1", around 220 pounds—not exactly what central casting would send for "man who eats 76 hot dogs." Meanwhile, some of the sport's most decorated competitors, including several elite female eaters, weigh in well under 130 pounds while still managing to inhale dozens of hot dogs (buns included) in the time it takes most people to finish one.

The prevailing theory is that stomach distension matters more than overall body mass—competitors train their stomachs to balloon temporarily to hold what would ordinarily require days to process, then return to normal size afterward. It's less about being a big person and more about having a uniquely cooperative stomach.

## Training Regimens That Would Alarm Any Nutritionist

Serious competitors reportedly:

- **Practice with water loading**, drinking large quantities to expand stomach capacity without the caloric consequences of practice hot dogs
- **Do "reps" with the actual food**, timing themselves on dozens of dogs to build both speed and technique
- **Fast strategically** in the days before competition to maximize empty stomach real estate
- **Perfect the "Solomon Method,"** named for eater Dale Boone, which involves splitting the hot dog from the bun and eating them separately, often dunking the bun in water to make it easier to swallow

## The Unglamorous Reality

For all the spectacle, competitive eaters describe grueling, almost ascetic preparation—it's less "fun contest" and more "controlled athletic event that happens to involve processed meat." Jaw muscles get sore. Competitors monitor hydration like marathoners. And somewhere, a very committed athlete is currently drinking a gallon of water while timing themselves with a stopwatch, dreaming of Nathan's famous stage.

The hot dogs, in the end, are almost beside the point.

# Nathan's Famous Hot Dog Eating Contest: A Legendary Rivalry Renewed

**CONEY ISLAND, New York (CNN)** — The scent of grilled franks and mustard hung thick in the July air Friday as competitive eating fans packed the Coney Island boardwalk for what many are calling the most anticipated Nathan's Hot Dog Eating Contest in years.

## The Chestnut Dynasty

Joey Chestnut, the sport's most dominant figure, arrived at this year's contest carrying the weight of expectation that comes with over a decade of near-total supremacy. Since claiming his first Mustard Belt in 2007, Chestnut has redefined what was once considered humanly possible, pushing the world record north of 70 hot dogs and buns in the 10-minute contest window.

His training regimen, long shrouded in a mix of showmanship and genuine sports science, reportedly includes jaw exercises, stomach-stretching techniques with water and cabbage, and meticulous attention to hydration and cardio conditioning in the days leading up to the event. Competitive eating insiders describe him as the "Tom Brady of hot dogs" — a competitor whose longevity has become as remarkable as his peak performances.

## The Kobayashi Question

Looming over the festivities, however, was the specter of Takeru Kobayashi, the Japanese eating icon whose six consecutive victories from 1997 to 2006 first brought the sport to international prominence. Kobayashi's early dominance — including a stunning debut that nearly doubled the existing world record — set the stage for competitive eating's explosion in popularity.

Kobayashi's relationship with Nathan's organizers has been complicated in recent years, marked by contract disputes and his eventual departure from the Major League Eating circuit. Any attempted comeback has been the subject of intense speculation among fans who remember the Chestnut-Kobayashi rivalry as the sport's golden age, when the two traded records and victories in front of growing television audiences.

Whether Kobayashi would appear at this year's contest — and under what circumstances, given past tensions with organizers — remained a storyline generating buzz throughout the buildup.

## Buildup and Spectacle

As always, the contest weekend featured its share of only-in-America spectacle: a weigh-in ceremony, trash talk from competitors representing multiple countries, and the traditional pageantry of the Nathan's Famous banner and belt presentation.

Crowds began gathering hours before the noon start time, with vendors hawking merchandise and longtime fans reminiscing about legendary contests past. ESPN's broadcast team prepared to call the action for viewers nationwide, continuing the network's decades-long partnership covering an event that has improbably become a Fourth of July tradition alongside fireworks and barbecues.

*This is a developing story.*
